articles.title: Missed cues, flightless fairies and big laughs in ‘Peter Pan Goes Wrong’
articles.text:
Missed cues, flightless fairies and big laughs in ‘Peter Pan Goes Wrong’ | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Margaret Clark as Tinker Bell and Jon Vellante as Peter Pan in "Peter Pan Goes Wrong." (Courtesy Miki Grubic)
Nobody staging a play expects everything to run amok. But that’s exactly what happens in the Lyric Stage Company of Boston’s wildly fun production of “ Peter Pan Goes Wrong,” running through Dec. 31. The show had the audience laughing out loud, and at the end of Act 1, a young theatergoer at the far right of the house exclaimed, “That was crazy!”
And she was right. The zany show-within-a-show is written by Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer and Henry Shields (“The Play That Goes Wrong”) and follows the Cornley University Drama Society. The not-so-great troupe of actors and crew members are staging Scottish playwright J.M. Barrie’s 1904 play “Peter Pan,” in which Peter takes Wendy Darling and her brothers, John and Michael, to Never Never Land. The production’s two directors, Robert (Kelby T. Akin) and Chris (John Kuntz) are both vying for the spotlight, belittling each other as they go. It’s clear that mayhem will ensue.
Elliot Norton Award winning director Paul Melone helms a show brimming with slapstick comedy, delivered by a very talented cast, several of whom do double and triple duty in multiple roles. Gabriel Graetz plays Francis, the narrator, who reads from Barrie’s book from a chair at either side of the stage as the actors embody — or try to embody — the characters. He also plays the pirate Cecco. Graetz, who recently starred in the hilarious “The Mystery of Irma Vep,” has a real aptitude for physical comedy and consistently brings the fun.
Kelby T. Akin, center, is Peter's shadow. (Courtesy Miki Grubic)
The entire cast is fantastic. Akin’s Robert also plays Nana the dog, Peter’s shadow and the wonderful Starkey, one of Captain Hook’s spirited, yet unintelligible pirates. Margaret Clark plays Annie, who portrays Mrs. Darling, Liza and Tinker Bell; Clark is also the show’s fight captain. Nora Eschenheimer is  brilliant as Sandra who playsWendy Darling. Brit Garner plays Gill, a Cornley stagehand and also a paramedic through Dec 20. Jenine Florence Jacinto is a reluctant Lucy who plays Tootles, Chris Kandra is Trevor the company’s stage manager, David Keohane is Dennis who portrays John Darling, a crab and pirate Mr. Smee, John Kuntz is Chris who portrays Mr. Darling and Captain Hook, Marc Pierre is a fabulous Max who portrays Michael Darling, mermaid and crocodile. Jon Vellante is Jonathan who portrays Peter Pan.
John Kuntz plays the role of Captain Hook. (Courtesy Miki Grubic)
Scenic designer Erik K. Diaz’s impressive rotating set, with three distinct scenes, brings the story’s worlds to life, with help from lighting designer Kevin Dunn, costume designer E. Rosser, sound designer and composer Alex Berg and wig designer Kat Shanahan. There’s a well-appointed bedroom with a triple bunk for the children, the ship where Captain Hook hatches his schemes and the forest of Never Never Land. But the real fun belongs to props artisans Lauren Corcuerra and Ernest Shao, props painter Mack MacIntyre, choreographer Ilyse Robinson, intimacy and fight director Ted Hewlett and, once again, Dunn.. Highlights include a memorable ocean scene full of painted sea-animal props held by cast members and bathed in moody lighting, a wonderful crocodile suit and all the makings of Pierre’s mermaid. There’s also a cheesy song and intentionally corny dance moves that elicited a lot of laughter from the crowd too.
So much in the show doesn’t go as planned. The spotlight is never in the right place. Peter Pan doesn’t fly and neither does Tinker Bell (although she does light up). Dennis can’t remember any of his lines, so they’re fed to him through a very visible headset. People get injured and nearly die. And that’s not all: There’s a love triangle, the crew accidently shares too many secrets and a lot of feelings get hurt. Despite repeated snafus, the show must – and does – go on.
And, sure, there are very few moments without hiccups. For anyone who isn’t into slapstick comedy, that might be far too many. But if you’re in need of a deep laugh, a scream or two of surprise – the audience let out a few on Thursday – and for life to feel a little lighter for a bit, “Peter Pan Goes Wrong,” just might be the answer.
The Lyric Stage Company of Boston’s production of  “ Peter Pan Goes Wrong” runs through Dec. 31.
Performing Arts
Jacquinn Sinclair Performing Arts Writer

articles.title: Remembering Charlie’s Kitchen, a Harvard Square fixture since 1951
articles.text:
Remembering Charlie’s Kitchen, a Harvard Square fixture since 1951 | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Customers chat with longtime waitress Helen Metros, center, in 2013. Metros worked at Charlie's for over 50 years. (Photo by Rick Friedman/Corbis via Getty Images)
Charlie’s Kitchen, a fixture in Cambridge’s Harvard Square since 1951, has closed for good. Owner and head chef David Toraji Oshima announced the closure on Facebook earlier this month, nearly 10 months after a flood from a dishwasher break shuttered the restaurant and after the building that housed it was sold.
“Everything was like, a little grime to it, the lock on the bathroom was always kinda falling off and the menus are like a little f—ing torn up,” said Daniel Carswell, a musician who booked shows at Charlie’s Kitchen from 2014 to 2022. “It was a place that had just been passed through a lot and was well-loved.”
Charlie's Kitchen in the 1970s. (Courtesy Cambridge Historical Commission)
Charlie Lambrose opened the restaurant at 10 Eliot St. in 1951. For decades, customers settled into its vinyl booths under neon signs for the famous double cheeseburger, grabbed cheap drinks in the beer garden, fed the jukebox and caught live shows on Monday nights.
The restaurant has been closed since January, when a malfunctioning dishwasher caused more than $2 million in water damage. A GoFundMe raised over $25,000 to support staff.
In October, Charlie’s held memorabilia sales, with proceeds going toward “finding a way to keep Charlie's Kitchen,” according to a post on the restaurant’s Facebook page.
Then the building was sold. Renato Valentim, a co-founder of the Tavern in the Square restaurant chain, bought the building for $2 million, according to state land records. Valentim did not respond to a request for comment.
“I would like to thank anyone and everyone who ate and drank at Charlie’s all these years, from the bottom of my heart. I’m sorry to have to give the community this sad news,” Oshima wrote in the statement.
Oshima, a chef and restaurateur who previously owned The Cornerstone in Somerville, which has since closed, began operating Charlie’s in spring 2024, taking over from Jaap and Paul Overgaag. “As a kid, I always remembered it being a fun burger place,” he said. Oshima bought the business in January 2025.
Oshima said he did a “complete 180” on the restaurant — everything but the double cheeseburger — upgrading the space, menu and service while running events such as trivia and karaoke nights. “We brought in some fresh faces to mix with the old faces and kind of help with that transition,” he said. “I brought in…some dishes from Hawaii that became pretty popular. There was a lot of skepticism, especially with my kitchen guys when we started doing it, but we started introducing things that they liked to make as well.”
Charlie's Kitchen was beloved for its vinyl booths, the famous double cheeseburger and cheap drinks in the beer garden. (Courtesy Mo Lotman)
The damage began on a January night when a dishwasher malfunctioned and failed to stop filling, sending water cascading through multiple floors. Because Oshima had moved the kitchen to the third floor, the flood traveled downward, damaging ceilings on the first and second floors and filling the basement. The water damaged the electrical system, leaving the building without power.
Oshima estimated that repairs and upgrades needed to reopen Charlie’s would cost about $2 million. But the biggest obstacle was insurance. Although Oshima received a few advances on the policy, the money went toward bills, he said. Neither he nor the previous landlord received the full insurance payout needed for repairs.
Oshima said he clung to the hope of reopening Charlie’s in its original location up until the building was sold. He said he made an offer but was outbid, and he didn’t learn the sale had closed until afterward. According to Oshima, the new owners had no interest in reviving Charlie’s.
“I really loved that kitchen, how it was set up and the guys in there that were cooking with me every day,” he said. “I'm going to miss a whole bunch about Charlie's.”
Teena Hallett, a social worker who focuses on harm reduction, worked at Charlie’s as a server and later a bartender from 2010 to 2016. “Charlie's was very no-frills. You could go in there looking however you wanted to look. You could get such cheap but good food. So it was really easy to go with a group of friends and hang out,” she said. “There were also karaoke and trivia nights, which were really popular with people. It was also, on the slower nights, a really good date spot.”
Hallett also pointed to the community that Charlie’s fostered and its faithful regulars. “During my time there, everyone I worked with had really good relationships with the people coming in,” she said. “We knew people's drink orders. We knew their names. We would talk to them about music. We had the jukebox on the second floor.”
Mo Lotman, author of “Harvard Square: An Illustrated History Since 1950,” called Charlie’s a fixture of the neighborhood, a familiar place where people from all walks of life passed through, from workers to students to punks. He credited its affordability and its welcoming, down-to-earth feel.
“There's a value to things having tradition and remaining constant and having a broad appeal and giving people an excuse to interact and hang out and have fun without the worrying about pretension and expense,” Lotman said.
Monday nights were for live music. Carswell first played a show at Charlie’s in May 2013, when promoter Ryan Agate was booking bands. “The regulars on Monday nights always had bands, so I would mark out one Monday a month for them to play a show with their pals,” Agate said. “It made the regulars feel even more of a part of the scene, and they got to live out their rock star fantasies.”

articles.title: Ending the dry stretch: Rain arrives late Sunday as fast-moving storm arrives
articles.text:
Ending the dry stretch: Rain arrives late Sunday as fast-moving storm arrives | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Southern New England hasn't seen a drop of measurable rain since Nov. 13, riding a pleasant streak of unseasonably warm temperatures too.
That tranquil stretch comes to an end later this weekend. Low pressure lifting off the Carolinas will tap into a stream of tropical moisture and track directly across southeastern New England late Sunday night, delivering a fast-moving but soaking dose of rain lasting into early Monday morning.
Here is what to know about the timing, the rainfall totals and why leftover autumn leaves could make the Monday morning commute a bit messy.
Predicted radar and cloud cover for Sunday at 11:30 p.m. (Danielle Noyes/1DegreeOutside)
Rain timeline
Saturday continues the streak of dry, mild weather before the atmosphere begins to moisten up ahead of the approaching cold front.
Sunday morning fog: Watch out for patchy fog forming overnight Saturday and turning locally dense around daybreak Sunday — especially in the typical low-lying locations
Rain arrival (5 p.m. — 7 p.m. Sunday): Rain overspreads the region from southwest to northeast right around dinner time on Sunday.
Heaviest downpours (8 p.m. Sunday – 3 a.m. Monday): The core of the storm moves through overnight, bringing steady, heavy rain with brief bursts around a quarter-inch per hour. Don't be surprised to hear a stray rumble of thunder around midnight.
Tapering off (7 a.m. – 9 a.m. Monday): The steadier rain winds down to scattered showers right during the heart of the morning commute, wrapping up completely by midday as mild afternoon air nudges back into the 60s.
Rainfall totals and clogged drains
Because this storm is progressive and moving at a brisk clip — and because the ground has had over a week to dry out — the risk for widespread flooding remains low.
Most of Southern New England: Expect 1 to 1.5 inches of rain, with isolated pockets approaching 2 inches in heavier downpours.
Southeastern Massachusetts: Slightly lower totals are expected here, generally 0.5 to 1 inch.
Likely precipitation accumulation ending Monday at 8 a.m. (Danielle Noyes/1DegreeOutside)
While rivers will handle this water easily, urban street ponding is a concern. Plenty of late-season fallen leaves are still sitting in neighborhood gutters and storm drains. Heavy rain overnight will easily clog up catch basins, creating deep puddles and slick hydroplaning spots for Monday morning drivers. If you have a storm drain in front of your house, Sunday afternoon is a great time to rake those leaves clear!
Coastal winds, rough seas and a cold snap
As the low pressure tracks nearby, winds will pick up out of the southeast overnight Sunday into pre-dawn Monday. The coast will see gusts of 30 to 35 mph, with 20 to 25 mph inland, before winds shift southwest and eventually west on Monday.
Predicted wave height for Monday at 7 a.m.(Danielle Noyes/1DegreeOutside)
Marine and tide impact: Offshore gusts will approach gale force, building seas to 10 to 13 feet Sunday night into Monday. Sheltered bays will get choppy, though it will be far calmer than the open ocean. Fortunately, the strongest onshore push aligns with Sunday evening’s lower high tide, and winds turn offshore before Monday’s higher mid-morning tide, keeping coastal impacts limited to minor splashover in the most vulnerable spots.
The chilly follow-up: Once this system clears out, a much colder air mass sweeps in. Tuesday's daytime highs won't get out of the low 40s. By Tuesday night, temperatures will tumble back to November reality, dropping into the 20s to low 30s.
Predicted low temperatures for Tuesday night. (Danielle Noyes/1DegreeOutside)
What about next week? New England should enjoy a quiet couple of days ahead of Thanksgiving, though there are signs that we get more active again potentially on Thanksgiving and into Black Friday too. Expect an update on Monday.
Danielle Noyes is a meteorologist for 1DegreeOutside and WBUR's go-to forecaster. For more weather insights, check out the free 1DegreeOutside app.

articles.title: Greater Boston is lighting up for the holidays. Here’s where to see the displays
articles.text:
Greater Boston is lighting up for the holidays. Here’s where to see the displays | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
The tree alight at the Boston Common Tree Lighting in 2024. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's Saturday morning newsletter, The Weekender. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox,  sign up here.
Bit by bit, nights in Boston are shining brighter. Yes, holiday light displays are beginning to flicker on around town and beyond.
Boston’s official Christmas tree is en route to its seasonal home on Boston Common. It’s expected to arrive on Nov. 24, but the city isn’t holding its lighting ceremony until Dec. 3. The good news is that zoos, gardens, parks and more are adding a bit of sparkle to their spaces before then, so you can get in on the spirit before the city’s official holiday lights go up.
For those who want to enjoy their fall and winter evenings with a smattering of twinkling lights, we’ve mapped out 11 of Greater Boston’s winter and holiday light displays. If you’re part of the “no holiday decor before Thanksgiving” crowd, just think of this as a preview to help you plan out your December. Below, you’ll find dates for each ceremony, so you can pencil a bit of brightness into your calendar over the next few weeks.
Stone ZooLights | Begins Friday, Nov. 20
149 Pond St., Stoneham
Thousands of lights transform the Stone Zoo into a glowing winter wonderland. This year’s installment features a new display in the zoo’s Yukon Creek, which includes North American animals like reindeer and Arctic foxes. General admission tickets are $19.95, and kids under the age of 2 get in free.
Faneuil Hall Christmas Tree Lighting | Saturday, Nov. 21
206 South Market St., Boston
Not to be confused with the city’s big annual lighting on the Common, Faneuil Hall is lighting its tree this Saturday at 6 p.m. with “help from Santa himself.” This light display is free to visit.
New England Botanic Garden Night Lights | Begins Saturday, Nov. 21
11 French Drive, Boylston
The New England Botanic Garden at Tower Hill’s winter display uses half a million lights to create a “Fantastical Forest.” Tickets for this event are timed, and prices vary for non-members. Standard nights are $26 for adults, $23 for seniors, $16 for kids aged 4 to 12. Peak nights are $29 for adults, $26 for seniors and $19 for kids. Children under 3 can get in free.
Columbus Park Trellis Lighting | Monday, Nov. 23
100 Atlantic Ave., Boston
Lights across the trellis in Christopher Columbus Park will go on at 5 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 23 and will stay on through April. This light display along the waterfront in Boston’s North End is free to visit.
Massachusetts Horticultural Society Festival of Trees | Begins Wednesday, Nov. 25
900 Washington St., Wellesley
The Massachusetts Horticultural Society’s annual “Festival of Trees” takes place at the Garden at Elm Bank in Wellesley. They’ll have themed trees donated by locals, model train displays and lightscapes across the garden. Tickets are timed, and peak pricing for non-members is $29 for adults and $10 for kids aged 3-17. Off-peak pricing is $24 for adults and $8 for kids. Children under 2 can get in free.
Martin's Park Ship Lighting | Saturday, Nov. 28
64 Sleeper St., Boston
This one’s for the kids. The ship at Martin’s Park in the Seaport transforms into a blue-and-white light display at 5 p.m. on Nov. 28. There will be cozy holiday beverages provided by Hood and Caffe Nero, craft activities, live holiday music and an appearance by Santa, who will arrive by boat with the Boston Police Harbor Unit.
Copley Square Christmas Tree Lighting | Monday, Nov. 30
560 Boylston St., Boston
Copley Square is lighting up its Christmas tree at 5 p.m. on Nov. 30. Santa will be in attendance; and there will be snacks provided by Hood and Drake’s Cakes. This event is free to attend. Visitors are invited to visit the Fairmont Copley Plaza after the lighting for cookies and pictures with Santa.
Boston Common Tree Lighting | Thursday, Dec. 3
139 Tremont St., Boston
Boston’s official Christmas tree lighting ceremony goes from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. on Dec. 3. You’ll hear from Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu as they discuss the history of the tree exchange. And just after the ceremony at 8:15 p.m., Wu will join the Friends of the Public Garden and other local organizations as they “flip the switch” to light up the Commonwealth Avenue Mall.
Boston's Annual Menorah Lighting | Sunday, Dec. 6
Opposite 68 Tremont St., Boston
Hanukkah begins on Friday, Dec. 4 this year. On the second night of the holiday, Chabad of Downtown Boston will light a 22-inch menorah at Brewer Fountain on Boston Common. There will be live music and local officials in attendance. This light display is free to visit, but organizers say RSVPs are appreciated.
Fenway Christmas Tree Lighting | Wednesday, Dec. 9
Opposite 77 Park Drive, Boston
Fenway’s neighborhood tree lighting will take place at the James P. Kelleher Rose Garden at 6 p.m. on Dec. 9. This light display is free to visit.
P.S. — Speaking of lights: After a monthslong restoration, Boston's Citgo sign was reilluminated this past Thursday. Take a look at history of this icon in this story from WBUR's Solon Kelleher.

articles.title: Local social club creates space for conversation and friends for those on the spectrum
articles.text:
Local social club creates space for conversation and friends for those on the spectrum | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Justice McPherson and Nicole Leontakianakos talk about Springboard Social Club. (Amanda Beland/WBUR.)
Loneliness is widespread in the U.S. with 1 in 3 adults reporting they feel lonely, according to the Centers for Disease Control.
One local nonprofit is particularly focused on people with autism. They can experience higher rates of isolation and fewer close friendships.
The Springboard Social Club in Greater Boston is doing something about it. It’s run by the organization Toward Independent Living and Learning and they bring together adults on the spectrum and people with learning differences to socialize.
Participant Justice McPherson is one of those adults.
“With these events, they kind of give you somewhat like an excuse to say, ‘I want to have fun, but I want to have fun with people,’” he said.
McPherson said Springboard has helped him communicate better with others on the spectrum, as well as those who aren’t autistic. Program coordinator Nicole Leontakianakos said her hope is that these activities help participants build relationships beyond Springboard.
“My measurement of success is that if my members are able to take the relationships they've built and then have those friendships outside of what we are organizing for them,” she said. “So if I find that a group has gone out to dinner without me there to facilitate, then I have done my job.”
She said she also wants to break the stigma that people on the spectrum don’t want to socialize.
“That's not the case,” she added.
WBUR Morning Edition host Tiziana Dearing spoke with Justice McPherson and Nicole Leontakianakos about Springboard and the benefits it provides them and others.

articles.title: The MBTA is planning fewer shutdowns in 2027. Here's a peek at the schedule
articles.text:
The MBTA is planning fewer shutdowns in 2027. Here's a peek at the schedule | WBUR News
Skip to main content
Support WBUR
Inside the Park Street MBTA station. (Robin Lubbock/WBUR)
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.
It's Friday! Shuttle buses are replacing Red Line service today through Sunday between Broadway and North Quincy. But the good news is weekday MBTA shutdowns should be fewer and farther between next year.
Here's what to know:
Planning ahead: For the first time since before the COVID pandemic, the MBTA averaged over 1 million weekday riders last month. And perhaps excitingly for its rebounding legions of riders, T announced yesterday it's planning fewer line outages in 2027. MBTA General Manager Phil Eng said it's a reflection of the progress the agency has made during all the closures in recent years. "As we continue to rebuild [and] renew our infrastructure, those days get less and less," Eng said during a MBTA board meeting. Click here — or scroll below — to see the full (tentative) closure schedule for 2027.
By the numbers: The schedule includes an even 100 days of 2027 outages. That's down from 132 days this year, 190 days in 2025, and a whopping 274 days in 2024. And of those 100 days, only 34 are weekdays.
The highlights: The first half of the year includes another big Green Line tunnel closure for nine days in January, a nine-day partial Orange Line closure in May and a 10-day closure of half the Blue Line in June. Eng said they're trying to schedule around holidays and weather. "In the winters, we try to stay in the tunnels," he told reporters after the meeting.
The work: The T's big projects for 2027 include finishing signal upgrades on the Red and Orange Line ( something they originally planned to finish this year) and getting the Green Line tunnel ready for the arrival of the first "supercars" next year — plus track maintenance and radio upgrades.
The MBTA's schedule of planned 2027 closures.
A breakthrough at BU: Researchers at Boston University are a step closer to being able to diagnose chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) while a person is still alive. Currently, the brain disease caused by repeated head trauma can only be diagnosed after death. But as WBUR's Amy Sokolow reports, a study published yesterday by the Boston University CTE Center found that a blood protein called eMTBR-tau was higher in people who had advanced CTE. Scientists said it opens the possibility of a blood test for CTE.
What's next: The hope is to begin moving toward FDA approval for a blood test within the next five years. But first, Michael Alosco, the director of clinical research at BU's CTE Center and study co-author, told Amy that more studies are needed to validate their findings.
Running it back: Suffolk County Sheriff Steve Tompkins is planning to run for another six-year term in 2028. The 69-year-old told the Bay State Banner this week that he was "pretty much thinking about retiring," but that his recent experience being a defendant in the criminal justice system made him reconsider.
Tompkins' office confirmed his decision in an email to WBUR: "His age is not a factor and ... he remains committed to helping people who are at the low ebb of life to regain their footing and improve their circumstances," a spokesperson for the sheriff said. "His work is unfinished and he has considerable energy to continue in his mission."
Wheels up: Logan Airport has begun experimenting with self-driving wheelchair-type vehicles — and plans to expand the pilot program next year. Massport CEO Rich Davey said yesterday that the autonomous tech is intended for people with mobility issues, as older adults make up a growing share of the population. At the same time, Davey said some customers have expressed "a discomfort" about needing a traditional wheelchair.
Zoom out: Autonomous wheelchairs have been used for several years at airports in Los Angeles and Miami. Here's a video of what they look like.
Lighting up: Boston's favorite petroleum ad (apologies, Memorial Drive Shell sign) is back. The rebuilt Citgo sign in Kenmore Square was illuminated last night for the first time since its $8 million relocation. You can watch the video of its relighting or read The New York Times story about what it all means.
